The European heatwaves, drought and wildfires led to more than 30,000 excess deaths, according to preliminary estimates, with national temperature records in at least eight countries, and major impacts on agriculture, energy and transport. An estimated 146.5 million people in India were exposed to extreme heat in an April 2026 heatwave. The Himalayan glacier collapse and catastrophic downstream flash flood in late August killed more than 1,300 people and had a massive impact on Nepal’s economy. Tropical cyclones caused devastation and loss of life in many countries. The current El Niño is expected to act as a risk multiplier for health. Increased heat, drought and heavy rainfall can contribute to heat-related illness and mortality, wildfire smoke and poor air quality, malnutrition and food insecurity, injuries, and changing risks of water- and vector-borne diseases such as cholera, malaria and dengue. The World Health Organization (WHO) has, for the first time, classified the anticipated health impacts as a health emergency. El Niño is already increasing risks for agriculture in key seasons and production systems, especially in areas where there is high food insecurity and heavy reliance on rainfed agriculture. Notes to Editors The nine global temperature datasets are: Berkeley Earth, CMA-GMST, CMST, DCENT-I, ERA5, GISTEMP, HadCRUT5, JRA-3Q, and NOAAGlobalTemp. This year’s report is accompanied by a new interactive online platform where users can explore the data behind the report, learn more about the methodologies, combine maps of climate data and explore El Niño. The platform is currently in beta, and user feedback is encouraged to support its further development. The World Meteorological Organization is the United Nations System’s authoritative voice on Weather, Climate and Water. It highlights the knock-on risks to the environment, economy, and everyday life. Key messages 2026 will be one of four warmest years on record El Niño turns up the heat and multiplies risks Sea level and ocean heat are at record high levels Extreme weather has massive economic and human cost Forecasts and warnings, underpinned by sustained observations, are vital Share: WMO 2027 Calendar Competition - Gaël Handschin The WMO State of the Climate Update 2026 shows that the past 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years being the top four. The global average surface temperature for January–September 2026 was about 1.47 °Celsius above the pre-industrial average. This figure is likely to rise through the end of the year because of the warming effect of El Niño, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December. Earth’s energy imbalance is rising and the earth system is accumulating heat at an accelerating rate. The imbalance reached its highest level since monitoring began, as greenhouse gases trap unprecedented amounts of heat and upset the equilibrium between incoming energy from the sun and outgoing energy. The ocean absorbs 90% of this excess heat and 2026 is on track to be the tenth successive year of record ocean warmth. Sea level is the highest on record, and sea-surface temperatures hit monthly records during 2026. The long-term retreat of glaciers continues - the annual mass loss of ice in 2025 would have filled five Olympic pools every second of the year. Freshwater storage has been dwindling since 2014. “We have entered a new age of climate extremes. A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst. Leaders must get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need.” said UN Secretary-General António Guterres. “ El Niño and indeed the state of the global climate in 2026 gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts. El Niño doesn't add new heat to the planet. It releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured. There is simply more heat available to release,” said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo . “We are supercharging our weather and El Niño will be a risk multiplier. Heatwaves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for. Hundreds of millions of people this year have been exposed to unbearable extreme heat, whilst the catastrophic ice and rock collapse and flash floods in Nepal highlighted the compound risks facing communities in fragile, warming high-mountain terrain.” Forecasts underpinned by sustained observations from every part of the world are more important than ever to monitor our rapidly changing climate and help navigate the increasing risks to societies and economies. The good news is that the number of countries reporting the existence of multi-hazard early warning systems (MHEWSs) has increased from 56 in 2015 to 136 in 2025, according to the report. The WMO State of the Climate 2026 Update was released on the first day of COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, as an authoritative, science-based report. It includes data – where available – up to September 2026 and therefore does not reflect the most recent impacts of El Niño. The final State of the Global Climate 2026 report will be issued in March 2027, incorporating scientific contributions from dozens of National Meteorological and Hydrological Services, regional climate centres, United Nations partners and experts from the WMO community. Highlights Global temperature: The global mean near-surface temperature anomaly averaged from January to September 2026 (1.47 °C ± 0.13 °C above the 1850–1900 average) is comparable to the whole-year averages for 2025 (1.43 °C) and 2023 (1.46 °C) and lower than the 2024 record (1.55 °C). This is based on nine internationally recognized datasets. The past four years, 2023-2026, are the four warmest years on record. La Niña conditions at the start of the year had a temporary cooling effect, which was reversed by the development of El Niño. Global monthly average sea-surface temperatures were the highest or second highest on record for June, July and August, and monthly global temperatures were among the three highest for the time of year from May to September. El Niño is forecast to continue into early 2027. El Niño typically boosts annual global mean temperatures by around 0.1 °C–0.2 °C, and it is likely that the final anomaly for 2026 will be higher than the January to September average. El Niño typically has the greatest impact on global average temperatures in the year after its development. Greenhouse gas levels reached a new record in 2025. Atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide has increased by 53% from around 278 parts per million (ppm) in 1750 to about 426.8 ppm in 2025. Global averaged methane concentrations increased from 729 parts per billion (ppb) in 1750 by 167% to 1 948 ppb in 2025. Nitrous oxide concentrations increased by 26% from 270 ppb in 1750 to 339.1 ppb in 2025. Measurements from benchmark monitoring stations (such as Mauna Loa in Hawaii and Kennaook/Cape Grim in Australia), indicate a continued increase in 2026. El Niño events typically lead to a surge in greenhouse gas concentrations. Earth’s energy imbalance: Ocean heat measurements and satellite observations show an acceleration in the rate at which the Earth system is accumulating heat. In 2025, it reached its highest observed value since monitoring began in 1960. Preliminary values for January–July 2026 suggest another record high. Ocean heat content in the upper 2 000 meters was the highest in the observed record in 2025 and has continued to rise in 2026, according to preliminary data (to July). Ocean warming rates have accelerated with a particularly strong increase over the past two decades, impacting marine ecosystems, biodiversity, and the ocean’s role as a carbon sink. Ocean heat intensifies tropical and subtropical storms, accelerates sea-ice loss in the polar regions, and – together with melting land ice – drives sea-level rise. This warming is projected to continue for hundreds to thousands of years. Global mean sea level reached a record high in 2026. Sea-level rise has accelerated since the start of the satellite record as a result of increased melting of glaciers and ice sheets, as well as increased thermal expansion of warming waters. June, July and August 2026 saw their highest values since the beginning of the satellite altimetry era in 1993. This sharp increase may reflect changes associated with the developing El Niño, including a shift in rainfall from land to ocean in the western tropical Pacific. Sea ice: In 2026, Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest annual maximum on record (in the satellite era since 1979), while the Arctic maximum was the lowest or second lowest. Sea ice plays an important role in the global climate system and polar ecosystems. Glaciers lost more than 400 gigatons of ice in 2025 - equivalent to approximately 1 mm of sea-level rise. This annual mass loss would have filled five Olympic pools every second of the year. 2025 marked the fourth consecutive year in which all 19 glaciated regions around the world suffered ice loss. The melting of glaciers has implications for local and downstream geohazards, ecology, regional water resources and water quality, as well as global energy and sea-level budgets. messages El Niño is firmly established and is expected to strengthen further WMO Forecasts show near 100% likelihood that it will persist through February 2027 Exceptionally warm tropical Pacific Ocean conditions support further intensification A very strong El Niño can significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide and fuel extreme weather WMO and National Meteorological and Hydrological Services step up preparedness and early-warning efforts for an exceptional event Full Report Press Release Factsheet As of mid-August 2026, El Niño has become firmly established, marked by persistent and intensifying positive sea surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific. The latest seasonal forecasts from WMO Global Producing Centres indicate an exceptionally high likelihood (nearly 100% probability) that El Niño will persist through September–November 2026 and December 2026–February 2027. Forecasts indicate further strengthening of El Niño in the coming months, with the event forecast to reach very strong intensity before peaking towards the end of the year. ENSO-neutral conditions or a return to La Niña are not anticipated during the outlook period. A very strong El Niño increases the likelihood of significant shifts in temperature and rainfall patterns in many parts of the world. However, the strength of an El Niño event does not translate directly into the magnitude of impacts in any region. About the El Niño/La Niña Updates series The El Niño/La Niña Update provides analysis of the current conditions and evolution of the status of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation phenomenon . These include detailed information on sea surface and subsurface temperature anomalies, atmospheric circulation, cloudiness and rainfall patterns. The Update is prepared through a collaborative effort between WMO and the International Research Institute for Climate and Society, with contributions from experts worldwide. The El Niño/La Niña Update is crucial for governments, humanitarian and disaster risk agencies, and policymakers to prepare for climate-related impacts and to provide guidance for meteorologists worldwide to refine regional predictions. src-cop31b-pbl-egr.title: UNEP Emissions Gap report 2026 | PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency
around: UNEP Emissions Gap report 2026 | PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency Skip to main content View the site in Dutch Nederlands PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency Home Menu Menu close Main navigation Home Latest Publications Topics Agenda About PBL Zoeken op trefwoord Search View the site in Dutch Nederlands Breadcrumb Home Publications UNEP Emissions Gap report 2026 New UNEP report lays out emission cuts needed for return to 1.5°C Report 21 October 2026 Energy and Climate Change UNEP Emissions Gap report 2026 to the report on the UNEP site to the newsitem Authors Specifications Related About the topic With global temperature rise set to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse emissions are needed to minimize the magnitude and duration of overshoot and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century, a new UNEP report finds. PBL Environmental Assessment Agency played a pivotal role in the modelling work. The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return looks at a ‘lowest possible’ 1.5°C overshoot scenario, in which peak warming by around the middle of the century is limited to 1.7-1.8°C and global temperature rise is returned to or below 1.5°C by 2100, with a 50 per cent chance. To get onto this pathway, relative to 2025 levels global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions would have to be reduced by 18 per cent by 2030, 45 per cent by 2035 and 69 per cent by 2040. This requires far deeper emission cuts than are projected under full implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) which only amount to 5-8 percent by 2030 and 11-15 percent by 2035, relative to 2025 levels.. The report shows many opportunities to accelerate action. Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement, renewable energy has boomed, total energy supply from coal and oil has grown slower than projected and climate policies have cut emissions in many places. Since the Paris Agreement, global renewable electricity capacity has grown three times faster than anticipated, with solar PV build- out increasing seven times faster. A continuation of these trends, supported by additional policies, would bring the world on track to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030 and increase the share of wind and solar in electricity generation to levels consistent with the lowest possible 1.5°C overshoot scenario. “Unfortunately we find that the target of 1.5 °C with limited overshoot is no longer possible. Our best scenario is now an overshoot of 1.7 or 1.8 °C by midcentury. On the other hand we see success stories that give reasons for hope. The growth rate of renewable technologies has surprised many. It shows that more progress is possible if governments are willing to step up their efforts,” says author Michel den Elzen of PBL Environmental Assessment Agency. Temperature projections still far too high The report finds that if current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8°C within this century and increase thereafter. If all NDCs are delivered and similar efforts continue, warming will be limited to 2.6°C. The latter outcome is worse than last year’s projections due to the withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions. New NDCs submitted since last year’s report have made a small difference for these projections. Even in the most optimistic scenario, where all NDCs plus additional net-zero targets are achieved, global warming would only be limited to 2.1°C in this century. Without urgent action, keeping peak warming below 1.7 to 1.8°C will quickly become impossible. Every five years of CO2 emissions at current levels pushes peak warming up by around 0.1°C. In addition, the lowest possible 1.5°C overshoot scenario creates a need for the removal from the atmosphere and permanent storage of roughly 320 gigatonnes of CO2 (equal to eight years of 2024’s global CO2 emissions) over the course of this century. This would be a huge effort. Copernicus said there is a 20 percent chance the year will tie or exceed 2024’s record and that global temperatures are virtually certain to exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels. The 2023–2026 average is also expected to top 1.5C. Nations are preparing to meet Monday for the two-week COP31 climate summit in Turkey. Key Facts Copernicus said the four-year average from 2023 to 2026 is expected to exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, the preferred limit set in the Paris Agreement. The world experienced its warmest October on record, with average global surface air temperatures 1.75C above the 1850–1900 pre-industrial baseline. Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, said October brought record global and surface ocean temperatures. The bulletin came after a year marked by deadly floods in Nepal, heatwaves in Europe and major wildfires in Indonesia. By AFP Published Nov 6, 2026 6:36 pm KST A person sits on the banks of the Seine River amid a severe heat wave in Paris, May 26. Reuters-Yonhap PARIS — The world is on track for 2026 to be the second-hottest year on record as an exceptionally strong El Nino weather pattern turbocharges human-driven global warming, the EU's climate monitor said Friday. This year still has a "20 percent chance of tying or exceeding" 2024 as the warmest ever seen, the Copernicus Climate Change Service said in a monthly bulletin. Global temperatures are now "virtually certain" to exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in 2026, Copernicus said. The four-year average from 2023 to 2026 is also expected to top 1.5C, the preferred limit set in the Paris Agreement to avert the worst impacts of climate change. The world experienced its warmest October on record, with average global surface air temperatures 1.75C above pre-industrial times, an era defined as 1850-1900, Copernicus added. "October has continued the pattern of remarkable global warmth, with record global and surface ocean temperatures," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which operates Copernicus. "An exceptionally strong El Nino is adding further heat to a climate already warmed by human activities," she said. The latest bulletin comes as nations prepare to meet on Monday for the U.N.'s two-week COP31 climate summit in Turkey after a year marked by deadly floods in Nepal, searing heatwaves in Europe and major wildfires in Indonesia.
